ASRSN:2161750.n: During my approach towards LXT I was monitoring CTAF and ADS-B. I was just east of the airport maneuvering to the NW to enter a right downwind for runway 36. I saw a plane SE bound just below my altitude that was closer to the airport than I was and they did not show up on ADS-B, they had not reported transitioning near the airport on CTAF. I diverted to the north to maintain separation.Implementing Class D airspace and a Control Tower would have helped identify this transiting aircraft and ensured better separation.
ASRSN:2161750.s: A pilot approaching LXT on a right downwind for Runway 36 diverted north to avoid a non-ADS-B aircraft that had not reported on CTAF. The reporter stated that implementing Class D airspace and a control tower would have improved separation.

ASRSN:2161754.n: Upon landing at U42 for recurrence training with another pilot. Our aircraft was on short final (less than a mile) and the other plane announced 'line up an wait runway 34' on the radio. That caused us to immediate execute a go around maneuver. During the go-around we monitored the position of the other aircraft visually and the other aircraft started (without announcing) a takeoff roll. As we were climbing we asked the other aircraft what was their intentions and they stated west departure. Traffic pattern was very busy at U42 with about 6 other planes in the traffic pattern and 4 others on the ground (according to our ADS-B in). After learning the other aircraft would be turning west we decided to exit the pattern turning east and returned to ZZZ1. I believe a Tower at U42 would be crucial to avoid things like this in the future.
ASRSN:2161754.s: Two pilots conducting recurrence training at U42 executed a go-around on short final after another aircraft announced "line up and wait" but then began an unannounced takeoff roll. The crew returned to ZZZ1 due to the busy traffic pattern, concluding that a tower is needed to prevent such conflicts.

ASRSN:2161759.n: I filed for an IFR trip from BFI and was assigned a GPS SID southbound. The SID calls for an initial climb to 700 MSL on compass heading, 'then direct to' first GPS fix (about 10 nm from the airport), then on compass heading for radar vectors. The instructions conclude with 'maintain 2000 or as assigned by ATC.' The chart depicts 700 on the leg from the airport to the first fix but, in the past, after handoff the departure controller has always followed up radar contact with a climb instruction to above 2000. This time the controller was busy and looking at the chart I somehow thought it was indicating that I should remain at 700 until the first fix. My mistake resulted in ATC calling a low altitude alert and instructing an immediate climb, which I did without further incident. There wasn't any obstacle issue at 700 and the weather was VMC, but this unnecessarily distracted the controller and could have been much worse if circumstances had been different. I know better, but in the distraction of the moment I didn't do what was logically intended in the SID. I think an improvement in the SID instructions would be 'then direct to cross (GPS fix) at or below 2000' to emphasize the expected uninterrupted climb and top altitude. This is in fact the verbiage for the northbound SID.
ASRSN:2161759.s: The pilot departed BFI on a GPS SID and mistakenly maintained 700 feet instead of climbing to 2000 feet due to misinterpreting the chart. This error triggered a low altitude alert from ATC, requiring an immediate climb, though no obstacles were encountered in VMC conditions.

ASRSN:2161764.n: The student entered the pattern for Runway 5 from a 45 degree entry. The first attempt at the short field approach and landing resulted in a go around due to being a little high and fast. The go around was uneventful and the student continued in left pattern for Runway 5. The second attempt for the short field approach and landing result in a satisfactory performance. After the touchdown, the student applied smooth aerodynamic braking and wheel braking. About 400' after touchdown, both the student and myself felt the left main wheel go flat and the student was able to maintain directional control, exit on Taxiway E, and bring the airplane to a safe stop.After exiting the airplane and inspecting the left main wheel, a screw/nail was seen in the tire. A person mentioned several airplanes had experienced flat tires in recent days when using Runway 5/23. No one injured.
ASRSN:2161764.s: A student pilot and instructor experienced a left main tire flat on a Cessna during the landing roll on Runway 5 after a short field approach. The tire was punctured by a screw or nail, but the student maintained directional control to a safe stop with no injuries.

ASRSN:2161777.n: On climb out from ZZZ we experienced engine roughness. I immediately turned around to land back at ZZZ. the roughness was periodic lasting about .5 seconds and 1 second between bursts. the engine was still running but I elected to come in high so power was not required to make the runway. I landed safely and was able to taxi off the runway and park.
ASRSN:2161777.s: The pilot experienced periodic engine roughness during climb out from ZZZ and immediately returned to land. The aircraft landed safely with high approach speed to avoid power requirements, allowing the pilot to taxi off and park without further incident.

ASRSN:2161779.n: My instrument student was under the foggles flying the aircraft while I scanned for traffic. We had called Razorback Clearance on the ground at VBT and requested flight following to ZZZ1. We departed runway 18 at VBT and began south. We tried to check on with Razorback on 126.6, but they were too busy to respond immediately. I saw a northbound aircraft on ADS-B IN that was 5 NM south of us and at our altitude (we were level at 2700 MSL). I told my student to maintain 2800 MSL to avoid the XNA Class C above us because we had not established 2 way radio communication with Razorback. As the traffic approached without losing sufficient altitude, I elected to take controls and climb up to 3000 MSL to avoid the traffic since I did not have them in sight. In doing so I busted the Class C without first establishing 2 way radio communication with Razorback. Razorback called us back as the traffic was passing below us, and we then proceeded to climb through the Class C airspace.
ASRSN:2161779.s: A flight instructor and student departed VBT and climbed to 3000 MSL to avoid traffic while unable to contact Razorback ATC. This maneuver resulted in an unauthorized entry into XNA Class C airspace before two-way communication was established.

ASRSN:2161793.n: I was PF with an instructor. Instructor was making position reports over ZZZ CTAF (upwind/downwind/final). We had come from ZZZ1 to ZZZ pattern and done 3 touch and goes and remained in the pattern. There was 3 other planes in the pattern when this event happened. We were approx 1/2 mile final when the aircraft in the pattern prior to us landed and exited the runway. My instructor had made a radio call that we were on final for runway XX for a touch and go. A plane announced they were entering runway XX 'to line up and wait'. My instructor announced we were short final but the airplane continued onto the runway. I executed a go around and side stepped to the right. The other plane started their takeoff roll and continued while I kept them in sight just below and to my left. On the upwind they kept straight. To prevent a collision and prevent entering the class B I turned right and left the pattern while my instructor made radio calls announcing our intentions. We decided to return to ZZZ1 as the pattern at ZZZ at that point had 5 aircraft.
ASRSN:2161793.s: The pilot and instructor executed a go-around and side-step maneuver when another aircraft entered the runway for takeoff despite the instructor's short final call. To avoid collision and Class B airspace, they exited the pattern and returned to ZZZ1 due to high traffic density.

ASRSN:2161794.n: Myself, was operating my drone in sea isle city New Jersey around XA00am on Day 0. I was on vacation, flying for recreational photography purposes. Before flight, I checked the 'Air Control' app to see if there were any restrictions or no fly zones. My flight area was clear and no restrictions. I visually inspected my flight zone and made sure there was no other traffic in the sky before flight. I was all clear. The flight area under my drone was clear. I then flew my drone straight up to 500m. Still clear and not interfering with any other traffic in the sky, there was nothing near me. I took a few photos remotely using my drones camera, hovered for a short time and rotated around to capture a few more photos before descending back down to under 400feet.I'm self reporting my flight deviation this evening because shortly after my flight, I posted a photo online and had a viewer question my flight altitude. After realizing that I made a mistake and flew past the allowed 400 feet, I came here to self report the flight deviation.Initially, I thought that since there was no flight restriction and the airspace was clear of all traffic, I could fly to what the software allowed for recreational purposes. But was completely mistaken.I did not have any collision, I did not encounter any other traffic in the sky, there were no close calls, no one was injured, and I never lost control or signal of my drone. I had full control during my entire flight. I just simply flew too high and returned to the proper flight altitude.
ASRSN:2161794.s: A recreational drone operator in Sea Isle City, New Jersey, flew a drone to 500 feet, exceeding the 400-foot limit, after mistakenly believing the clear airspace permitted higher altitudes. The operator self-reported the deviation, noting no traffic conflicts, collisions, or loss of control occurred during the flight.

ASRSN:2161820.n: Terminal A has changed the ramp design and markings south of the terminal nearest the Old Terminal A Building. We were given taxi instructions inbound after crossing 22R at N. Our instructions were to use A10 to A9 park [gate] XX. As I've done this many times and had the chart out I looked for the transition to A9, but it was blocked by cones. I then saw a taxiway further west that L1, where there is usually a fence. Then I noticed the fence was basically gone, moved all the way back to the old Terminal A building. As I transitioned to A9, the line had clearly been scrubbed from the concrete surface. A9 was gone. There was another parallel taxi line that used while we asked Ramp where A9 was. They said where we were was fine. On my Jeppesen AMM I was now taxiing in a closed red boxed area. As there was never any bulletin issued and I had NO prior knowledge of this change being in an uncharted area was very unnerving and potentially dangerous. Nothing happened, as we parked moments later, but the confusion of it all was high.
ASRSN:2161820.s: The pilot reported taxiing inbound at Terminal A where uncharted ramp design changes and removed markings caused confusion. Although the aircraft parked safely after consulting Ramp, the pilot found the lack of prior notice regarding the closed area potentially dangerous.

ASRSN:2161848.n: During taxiout from terminal A Ramp tower cleared us to taxi 'A8, left on F3'. The current Taxi diagram for EWR does not have the new depiction of the taxiways. F3 is on the old terminal B. We stopped the aircraft and asked for clarification. Flight continued without further incident. Pushed off the gate onto A10 line. When ready for taxi, was given A10, F3/A8. Was told F3 is a new taxiway to the left as we exited (there was a F3 to our right as we exited but that wasn't what ramp wanted us to use. This IS NOT depicted on either the AMM (Airport Moving Map) or the 10-9 chart. There was no training bulletin or ops alert as to this change and after I stopped to query which way to go we turned onto the UN MARKED taxiway that took us into the red hash marks (non-taxi area) on the AMM to hold short of A8 and contacted ground there. This is simply not safe until the crews are informed of this new taxiway to get out of Terminal A. Should be a message, bulletin and company communication on this ASAP and ramp control should be much more helpful with this changed. The old taxiways L3, L2 and L1 are still there and there were only 3 cones on them - if they are closed now, there should be cones across the whole taxiway.
ASRSN:2161848.s: The pilot reported that during taxiout from Terminal A at EWR, Ramp Control issued a clearance for a new, unmarked taxiway F3 not depicted on charts or the Airport Moving Map. The crew stopped to clarify, inadvertently entered a non-taxi area, and contacted Ground Control before continuing safely, citing a lack of training and proper signage as the cause.

ASRSN:2161867.n: On visual approach to runway 28L in SFO, approach directed flight to maintain 180 KIAS to five mile final and contact tower. Shortly after contacting tower, in VFR conditions and on the PAPI, the tower issued a low altitude alert. As PM I acknowledged the alert with present altitude. Just as I was speaking with tower the Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS) alerted stating 'flaps.'As I double checked the configuration and altitude I noticed we were at 800AGL, in VFR, on the PAPI glide path and moving the flaps from 15 to 30. The flaps were double checked to have reached 30, landing checklist completed before 600 AGL. Flight continued to uneventful landing.The EGPWS was simply Flaps and NOT Too Low Flaps. The aircraft was stable at 500AGL so approach was continued to landing.
ASRSN:2161867.s: During a visual approach to SFO runway 28L, the crew received a tower low altitude alert and an EGPWS "flaps" warning at 800 AGL while moving flaps from 15 to 30. The crew confirmed the configuration, completed the landing checklist by 600 AGL, and continued to an uneventful landing.

ASRSN:2161887.n: We were flying ZZZ1-ZZZ2. First Officer (FO) was the pilot flying and I was pilot monitoring (PM). The weather was VMC. At top of cruise I noticed a faint electrical odor in the galley area. My FO also agreed he smelled a faint odor. At the time it was not enough to cause alarm but we started the process of trying to determine the source. After approximately 45 minutes we ran the non-alert Smoke/Fire/Fumes checklist which had us remove power from the galley area via the Cab Bus Switch. Over the next 5 minutes the odor became more pronounced. Not being able to determine the source, we decided to divert. We donned O2, informed ATC of our intention to divert to ZZZ. They gave us vectors and a descent. I sent a divert message via ACARs and set up the ILS Y XXL to ZZZ. We [requested priority handling] and reported our fuel and souls to ATC. At this time I decided to become pilot flying (PF) and the FO became PM. He obtained landing data for XXL where we realized XXL had been shortened to 7000. We were able to get MAX numbers so we continued. We had ZZZ in sight from 25 miles out but we were unable to tune the ILS. The ILS had been NOTAMd out for XXL. We asked Tower if they could turn on the ILS and they said it was unavailable. We had guidance from the NAV/PROF as well as the VASI for XXL. We landed uneventfully. After landing we determined we were unable to 180 on the 150 wide runway or taxi off on 1 due to weight restrictions. We made the decision to run the evacuation checklist and exit the aircraft on the runway. I blew the slide. The galley area now had visible haze and very pronounced electrical odor. Once the slide was deployed I exited the aircraft and my FO followed behind. The slide is very steep and very fast. My FO injured his hip during his dismount at the bottom. The whole experience was very slow developing. I found that it was hard to make the divert decision due to the slow onset with no associated indications. Once the divert decision was made the process becomes much tougher with the oxygen mask and goggles. My FO and I had outstanding CRM throughout the entire process. That open loop decision making enabled us to keep a very high level of safety throughout the flight. We have flown together several times. We had been using the technique of having divert fields in the fix page. At the time of the divert we had ZZZ3 and ZZZ and decided upon ZZZ due to familiarity with the airfield. Reading the NOTAMs prior to the divert decision would have helped immensely. Obviously this would need to be done well in advance of the actual divert.
ASRSN:2161887.s: The Captain and First Officer diverted a ZZZ1-ZZZ2 flight due to a worsening electrical odor and haze in the galley. After landing on a shortened runway with an unavailable ILS, they evacuated via slide, resulting in the First Officer sustaining a hip injury during dismount.

ASRSN:2161941.n: First Officer's Take off, Seconds into the takeoff roll on runway 31 my FO states, (paraphrasing) 'I can't control the airplane.' Initially I was puzzled because everything looked and felt normal to me. He then stated (paraphrasing), 'I have full left rudder and can't hold the center line.' The inflection in his voice indicated he was dead serious. Suspecting a flight control problem, I responded with 'Reject, I have the aircraft.' Control of the aircraft was transferred back to me. I could feel the asymmetry in the rudder pedals with the left pedal all the way to the floor. We conducted a low-speed RTO at approx. 60 knots. We exited the runway onto taxiway 1 and conducted the RTO (Rejected Takeoff) and after landing checklist. My FO stated he felt the aircraft wanting to aggressively drift to the right on takeoff and he had the left rudder pinned to the floor to maintain control. My hand was on the tiller at the time, but control input was minimal, if any. In no way, shape or form did I feel I was counteracting a hard rudder input with the tiller. We coordinated with ground control to park in a place in which we were not in anyone's way. We contacted operations and asked our dispatcher to patch a 3-way call to Maintenance Control. During the conference call my FO spoke with Maintenance Control so he could accurately describe firsthand what he felt the aircraft was doing. Maintenance Control recommend going back to the gate for a series of inspections. After block in we spoke with the duty officer and made a MEL write up. Cause: Unknown. The MX inspections did reveal anything outside normal parameters. Suggestions: Considering the unexpected nature of the event, the critical phase of the flight and compressed time frame (seconds) to observe, orientate, decide and act I feel we did a good job. My FO, based on 12000 hours of flight time, felt something didn't seem right and feel right. He did the right thing by speaking up in an assertive manner. This was the first time in my career I've had a First Officer state 'I can't control the aircraft;' on his take off roll. I felt the correct response on my part was not 'Continue' but instead 'Reject, I have the aircraft.' We were below 80 knots (low speed regime). Delaying the RTO (Rejected Takeoff) to diagnose the problem while accelerating would have created more jeopardy. I realize my RTO (Rejected Takeoff) and our block-turn-back created significant delays. Additionally, it tied up a lot of men and resources to do their due diligence and inspections. I'm aware. However, our actions reflected what we are taught in training. At the end of the day a lot of people were inconvenienced but there was no bent metal and no injuries.
ASRSN:2161941.s: During a First Officer's takeoff roll on runway 31, the crew rejected the takeoff at 60 knots after the First Officer reported an inability to control the aircraft due to full left rudder input. Maintenance inspections found no mechanical faults, leaving the cause unknown, though the crew successfully executed a low-speed RTO with no injuries.

ASRSN:2162063.n: There was a near midair collision while on the ILS 34R approach into AFW. There were two pilots in our aircraft. I was the instructor and the left seat pilot was also a Multiengine Instructor receiving a proficiency flight. We were on an IFR flight plan from ZZZ1 to AFW. We received vectors early on for the ILS34R and we were in the clouds for a majority of the time in the air. We were established on glideslope for the ILS 34R and cleared for the approach. As we were descending via the glideslope beyond the final approach fix we got a warning from Tower and ADSB that an aircraft was turning towards us. We were in the clouds still with no visual of the aircraft. I took controls of the aircraft applied full power and pitched up to gain altitude and separation from the aircraft at the same time that tower called and told us to maintain altitude. The aircraft appeared to be within several hundred feet vertically and horizontally on the ADSB. Initially the aircraft appeared to be flying away from the approach course but turned towards the path. The other aircraft appeared to be just below the cloud layer. Tower recleared us to land and we were still established on the glideslope and continued the approach. We broke through the clouds approximately 200ft lower and landed safely at AFW. Tower was trying to contact the aircraft as it turned towards the ILS final approach course, but did not get a response. This prompted to look closely at the ADSB traffic output. As I saw the aircraft turning towards us I prepared to level off or climb. As the aircraft continued the turn we initiated the evasive maneuver as ATC was also contacting us to stop the descent. This experience is a reminder to maintain vigilance even when you are in the IFR system and receiving traffic separation services. We had no visuals as we were in instrument meteorological conditions, but the ADSB traffic system gave us an advance warning. Moving forward I will continue to maintain vigilance in a traffic scan even if I am in instrument meteorological conditions. Crew resources were utilized effectively on this flight and I believe having a pilot flying and another pilot monitoring allowed us to avoid a more serious incident.
ASRSN:2162063.s: Two instructors in an aircraft on an ILS 34R approach into AFW executed an evasive climb after ADSB and Tower warned of a non-responsive aircraft turning toward their path in IMC. The crew maintained separation, broke clouds at 200 feet, and landed safely after Tower recleared the approach.

ASRSN:2162067.n: While attempting to expedite our descent (at ATC request) into LAS, we encountered wake turbulence in the trail of a Boeing 777. This led to a roll right and left each of 40 degrees and a loss of altitude of about 250 feet. After correcting, we requested a deviation away from traffic to left-offset the 777's flight path. We were granted some relief, but soon found ourselves back in trail as we entered the CHOWW TWO STAR. Due to this, when we first started on the CHOWW 2, we needed more clarity about our assigned altitude. The Controller instructed us initially to level off to allow the 777 to get below us but then promptly assigned us a descend 'via.' This initially led to us being off course and high at the beginning of the STAR. Compounding this was the request from ATC to declare any injuries or damage to our aircraft and, finally, another Controller handoff.One of the final Controllers estimated that we would not be able to reach our next assigned altitude as we approached TATUU on the CHOWW 2. When we attempted to expedite our descent to comply, we pushed the nose too far over and attained a speed of 264 knots in a 250 knot restricted airspace. We never entirely made it to the point in question (TATUU) as we were vectored off the STAR by ATC. We were then advised of possible pilot deviation and given a number to call.Where I screwed up: Following the wake turbulence event, I acknowledge that we should have IMMEDIATELY requested vectors away from the STAR and sought ATC assistance. It shook us up, and we were overwhelmed by continual turbulence as we stayed behind the 777 down the chute. It compounded our already heavy workload, and we were reluctant to descend into the wake turbulence again for fear of injury or damage to our aircraft.
ASRSN:2162067.s: The flight crew encountered wake turbulence from a Boeing 777 while descending into LAS, causing significant roll and altitude loss. Subsequent confusion with ATC instructions and an expedited descent attempt resulted in an airspeed violation and a potential pilot deviation report.

ASRSN:2162088.n: Between 10-15 miles north of ZZZ, I received the AWOS. I don't remember the wind direction, but others were using Runway XX, so I entered at approximately a 45-degree angle. I was #1 to land and there was someone waiting to depart. I had the impression that I was too high and I saw hills, so I didn't feel comfortable descending. When I turned final I was too high and I tried to descend. I gained more speed than I intended and was probably too fast. When I turned final I was at approx.76 knots and 1500rpm. I pushed the yoke forward to reduce altitude. When I rounded out and tried to touch down, I bounced two to three times. I taxied off the runway and parked in front of the FBO. When I inspected the aircraft I noticed the propeller was bent. I then called my instructor.
ASRSN:2162088.s: The pilot reported a high-speed approach and bounce landing at ZZZ due to being too high on final, resulting in a bent propeller. The aircraft was taxied off the runway and parked after the incident.

ASRSN:2162094.n: Demo flight of UAS was conducted close to our metal building on private property, and it interfered with the remote signal on the UAS. The UAS overshot its return to home function by several feet, and broke 2 propellers and an engine before dropping from 15' to ground. No injury or near misses sustained.
ASRSN:2162094.s: During a UAS demo flight near a metal building, signal interference caused the drone to overshoot its return-to-home function. The aircraft broke two propellers and an engine before dropping from 15 feet to the ground with no injuries.

ASRSN:2162095.n: I operated a drone greater than 55lbs without the proper waiver/permissions. I am a member of my local Search and Rescue (SAR) team where I operate as a sUAS pilot. We deploy drones on just about every callout and have been very successful in saving lives. We have been so successful that we got the attention of the drone manufacturer. The Drone manufacturer reached out to us to ask if we would be willing to test their delivery drone, as a SAR asset. We of course accepted and the manufacturer shipped us a Demo unit. With all the excitement of the new drone showing up, our Sheriff setup a demo for a few of the commissioners. We conducted this demo at a trailhead in the foothills of the mountains. I flew the drone up to 100' AGL and performed a quick demo of the winch system and it was conducted in VMC and in Class G airspace. I have hence learned that I flew the drone illegally and without the proper waiver that is needed. With my years of aviation experience I know that regulations are there to ensure the safe operation of aircraft and should have been more diligent to operate appropriately. I will not fly the drone again until I have the proper permission to do so and will be more diligent in the future to ensure all regulations are followed.
ASRSN:2162095.s: A Search and Rescue sUAS pilot illegally operated a delivery drone weighing over 55 lbs up to 100 feet AGL in Class G airspace without the required waiver. The pilot acknowledged the violation, ceased operations, and committed to obtaining proper permissions before future flights.

ASRSN:2162105.n: Aircraft X departed RDM runway heading off of Runway 5, assigned 140 for altitude. Tower had Aircraft Y depart east bound. I was not talking to either aircraft until the conflict was resolved, but they nearly merged at the same altitude (around 5,400 ft, below my MIA). It appeared Aircraft X and Aircraft Y got each other in sight at Aircraft Y turned slightly northeast to parallel Aircraft X, but they got to within maybe .1 miles at the same altitude. The pilot didn't say NMAC but it was definitely a NMAC. It appeared that Aircraft X stopped climbing to avoid Aircraft Y for a moment. It is so smoky in the area with all of the wildfires, it is very difficult to get traffic in sight. I tried issuing a southbound vector in the blind to the Aircraft X and tried calling traffic in the blind, but they were still on Tower frequency. Tower told my d side training team that they issued instructions to the aircraft to resolve the situation, but it was definitely one of, if not the closest calls I've had. The fact that Redmond Tower has passenger jets and other aircraft and all the other nearby airports with no radar in the Tower renders them incapable to safely navigate aircraft in and out of the area, and it is only a matter of time before there is a midair collision that could be prevented. This sector is designed to fail. As long as it is not a class C and Tower does not have a radar, we are going to watch a lot of people die one day, and I hope I am not working when it happens. It is unsafe and no one at ZSE is suited to work the airspace.
ASRSN:2162105.s: An air traffic controller reported a near midair collision between Aircraft X and Aircraft Y at approximately 5,400 feet near RDM, where the aircraft merged within 0.1 miles. The controller attributed the incident to wildfire smoke reducing visibility and the lack of radar at Redmond Tower, which they claim renders the sector unsafe.

ASRSN:2162108.n: Aircraft X flew the rnav34 to s33 IFR. Instead of flying northbound to gashe, as published, they flew ENE. I tried calling them in the blind and no joy. Eventually I reached them and asked them if they had cancelled IFR and they said they were still IFR. I asked why they weren't flying the published missed approach and they said they forgot. I issued a low altitude alert and told them to 'Join the published missed approach' and climb when they were below the MIA. It is my understanding that joining is at the pilot's discretion, and I didn't want to issue a direct clearance or let them continue heading towards higher terrain away from a flight checked area like the missed approach. I issued a pilot deviation to the pilot.The aircraft was deviating from assigned headings AFTER this issue as I vectored them for their next IFR approach.Every shift it seems like there are pilot deviations in the redmond area. It is one thing if its a solo student, but these are with instructors on board with little to no visibility in the smoke. I don't know how to make these flight school pilots fly their aircraft as cleared by ATC.
ASRSN:2162108.s: An ATC controller reported that Aircraft X, flying an RNAV34 to S33 IFR, deviated from the published missed approach by heading ENE instead of northbound because the pilot forgot the procedure. The controller issued a low altitude alert, instructed the pilot to join the published missed approach, and filed a pilot deviation report.

ASRSN:2162142.n: On base leg for XXC got a TCAS RA moments after traffic called out to us. We were level at 4000' and got an RA to level off for traffic below us at 3600 ft. After disengaging autopilot and auto throttles we leveled at 4100 ft and got the clear of traffic response. We reported to ATC our altitude after reporting TCAS RA. Maneuvering on left base to ZZZ Rwy XXC, at 4000' MSL, heading 180, 210k received TCAS RA. Disconnected autopilot and autothrottles, climbed 100' to resolve conflict, which was climbing from about 3600'MSL below and ahead.
ASRSN:2162142.s: The flight crew on base leg for XXC received a TCAS RA while level at 4000' due to traffic climbing from 3600' below. They disengaged autopilot and autothrottles to climb 100 feet, resolving the conflict and receiving a clear of traffic response.

ASRSN:2162150.n: Due to performance, we required Runway XXR. After reaching XXR we were cleared for takeoff did normal procedures entering the runway and starting the takeoff role. At approximately 80 to 90 kts we heard a loud pop and felt a vibration through the airplane. The Captain announced rejecting take and did the reject procedure. I notified Tower that we were aborting. I verified with the Captain that he wanted Air Fire Rescue called for. He said yes, I made an immediate second radio call verifying the aborted takeoff and requesting emergency equipment be dispatched to our location. We made the remain seated, remain seated PA, and the Captain brought the aircraft to a stop on high-speed Taxiway 1. We then ran the rejection takeoff checklist. Air Fire Rescue equipment showed up and verified that we had blown both right main tires. They notified us that they called Ops and had buses and Maintenance in route to our location. The Captain then briefed the Flight Attendants, after which he briefed the customers. I notified Ops and Maintenance. Maintenance requested that we do an ELB (Electronic Logbook) report and I accomplished the ELB report immediately. Then the Captain called Dispatch and notify them of our situation. The Captain made several PAs to the customers and kept them calm. Approximately 20 minutes later, the buses showed up Air Fire Rescue brought the air stairs up to the airplane, and we deplaned the customers and they were taken to the terminal. All customers were deplaned in an orderly manner. They all appeared to be happy with an upbeat mood and there were no injuries. Normal taxi out to Runway XXR. After being cleared for departure, takeoff roll began normally at around 80 to 90 kts we heard a loud bang and then felt airframe vibration. Rejected takeoff call was made by me. The reject procedures were accomplished. Tower was notified of the rejection and the crew requested Crash, Fire, and Rescue to be rolled. After maintaining directional control and slowing the aircraft to an appropriate taxi speed, the crew attempted to clear the active runway, however due to the vibration, the crew deemed it was more prudent to stop the aircraft on the high-speed [Taxiway] 1. Upon arrival, the rescue unit determined that the right main tires were damaged. A thermal sense check was accomplished by the Fire Department and deemed the temperatures were below any fire threat. A multilevel coordination then began between Dispatch, Maintenance, Operations and the crew. The passengers were deplaned via buses and taken back to the terminal. The aircraft was then handed over to Maintenance with the appropriate write ups in the ELB (Electronic Logbook).
ASRSN:2162150.s: The flight crew rejected takeoff on Runway XXR at 80–90 kts after a loud pop and vibration caused by blown right main tires. The aircraft stopped on high-speed Taxiway 1, where Fire Rescue confirmed no fire threat, and all passengers were safely deplaned without injury.

ASRSN:2162158.n: While descending on the WYNDE Arrival into ORD passing around 26,000 ft., the left wing dropped and the aircraft banked to 30° to the left. Roll authority was annunciated and the autopilot was disengaged from this action. Pilot flying intervention preceded and corrections were made before reengaging automation. ATC was notified. Crew then slowed and offset course to avoid any additional wake turbulence.
ASRSN:2162158.s: During descent on the WYNDE Arrival into ORD at 26,000 ft, the aircraft banked 30° left due to wake turbulence, disengaging the autopilot. The pilot flying corrected the attitude, notified ATC, and offset the course to avoid further turbulence.

ASRSN:2162274.n: This occurred at XA55Z on frequency 126.5We were vectored for a RNAV 28 approach. Our intention was to start out on the approach and then cancel IFR and proceed visually since the weather is clear in HDN. We were instructed to cross HIPPA at or above 13000 and cleared for the approach. We set the FAF altitude of 10000 in the alt selector. The problem is we did not engage VNAV and we went below the 13000 altitude to about 12,200. No terrain warnings were set off. The controller told us we went below his minimum vectoring altitude. We corrected the altitude and then cancelled IFR and landed uneventfully. Suggestion: Better vigilance on engaging the correct vertical modes might have prevented this mistake.
ASRSN:2162274.s: The flight crew descended below the 13,000-foot minimum vectoring altitude while vectored for a RNAV 28 approach at XA55Z due to failing to engage VNAV. The controller alerted them to the deviation, after which they corrected altitude, cancelled IFR, and landed uneventfully.

ASRSN:2162279.n: On Day 0, flight crew on Company Aircraft X ZZZ to ZZZ1 shut down engine 2 in the air after takeoff due to low oil pressure. Around 1200ft agl Flight crew had a master warning indicating low oil pressure. The Captain turned to the system page and identified that the engine 2 oil pressure was indicating 30 psi. Using PIC and Captain's authority, the Captain decided it was best to shut down the engine. The flight crew identified the affected engine and shut down engine 2. After securing the engine the flight crew [requested priority handling] with ATC. Company dispatched and ground operations were advised of the [priority handling] aircraft by the flight crew. The Flight Attendant and passengers were advised by the PIC of what has happened and the intentions of the crew. Flight crew told ATC that they wanted to return to ZZZ. While being vectored for the ils XXL into ZZZ the aircraft had a miss trim master caution. Crew ran the checklist and turned the autopilot back on which then created a large yawing action and full rudder deflection by the autopilot. The Captain disconnected the autopilot and hand flew the aircraft. At this time the flight crew requested to come straight in for the ILS XXL. Flight crew was aware that this would cause them to touch down over max landing weight. Flight touched down smooth and safely on the runway with the use of minimal breaking. Emergency vehicles follow the aircraft to inspect and make sure the aircraft was in a safe condition. At the time of touchdown the aircraft was 100 pounds over max landing weight. Aircraft was able to taxi to the gate under its own power and safely deplane the passengers.Cause: Lack of oil in the engine.Suggestion: An increase in maintenance procedures for checking engine oil. After takeoff on Runway XXL from ZZZ, operating as Company Aircraft X, the aircraft was climbing through 1200 feet AGL on a 060 heading. We received a low oil pressure warning for the #2 engine. We turned to the system page and identified that the engine 2 oil pressure was indicating 30 psi. Using PIC authority and CRM, I decided it was best to shut down and secure the engine. The flight crew identified the affected engine and shut down engine 2 using SOPs. After securing the engine, we [requested priority handling] with ATC and received a vector for the downwind. Company Dispatch, the Flight Attendant, and ground operations were advised of the [priority handling] by the flight crew. The cabin was advised of the situation and that we were returning to the field. We advised ATC of our plan to return to ZZZ, but we were currently overweight and needed to burn fuel for roughly 20 minutes. While being vectored to burn fuel, the aircraft had a mistrim master caution for the rudder. We ran the electronic checklist for the mistrim, and after disengaging, retrimming, and reengaging the yaw dampener, this created a large yawing motion and near full rudder deflection by the yaw dampener. As the pilot flying, I disconnected the yaw dampener and hand-flew the aircraft. We were aware that we were still overweight by around 100 pounds over our maximum landing weight, but with the malfunctioning yaw dampener, we made the decision to head directly to the airport and initiate the approach for XXL. The aircraft touched down smoothly and safely on the runway and used minimal braking. Emergency vehicles were waiting to inspect us after exiting the runway, they didn't notice anything on the exterior to be a hazard and cleared us to taxi back to the gate. We offloaded the passengers into the terminal after securing our ground crew and equipment.Cause: Upon later inspection, the mechanic found the #2 engine to be approximately 8 quarts low on oil. I'm not aware of the servicing record for the oil prior but the mechanic that inspected said it must have been overlooked or maybe serviced while the oil was too hot. Suggestions: I think there should be a more standard way of servicing the oil, more exact than current. Have a set amount of time to cool and settle before servicing maybe.
ASRSN:2162279.s: Flight crew on Company Aircraft X shut down engine 2 after takeoff due to low oil pressure caused by insufficient oil. During the return, a mistrim caution triggered a yawing motion when the yaw dampener was re-engaged, forcing a manual landing 100 pounds over maximum weight.

ASRSN:2162293.n: Climbing through FL 280, M.79, aircraft experienced a sharp jolt that yawed the aircraft approximately 5 degrees left followed by a severe long period vibration that lasted for 20 to 30 secs. Divert to ZZZ1.NUMBER 5 BEARING IN RIGHT ENGINE FAILURE causing compressor stall.
ASRSN:2162293.s: During climb through FL 280, the M.79 experienced a sharp jolt and severe vibration caused by a right engine failure and compressor stall. The crew diverted to ZZZ1 due to the failure of number 5 bearing.

ASRSN:2162294.n: This event really started prior to our flight to ZZZ. Uneventful landing in ZZZZ, brakes heated up as they always do in ZZZZ. Turned brake fans on prior to gate arrival. Aircraft boarded for on time departure. After 45 minutes of brake fans on, noted brake temps as 45 40 215 40. Called maintenance to check #3 brake and brake fan. Maintenance said brake fan working, temp is under the 300 limit and signed off as Ops Check OK. After take off received auto brake ECAM which instructs crew to calculate landing distance and use manual baking. No big deal. The FO made a stabilized approach and normal landing on XXL. Around 90kts he applied braking as to make the last high speed turn off. The aircraft abruptly veered 30 degrees to the left, I took the aircraft and was able to stop the aircraft before runway excursion occurred. Slowly taxied to gate a wrote up right side brakes not as effective as left side. On taxi in noted bake temps now indicating 365 295 80 560Looking back, I should have refused the aircraft in ZZZZ even though it received a maintenance sign off. The mechanics were correct that the brake temp of 215 was legal, but it was obvious that there was something wrong with the temps indicating 45 40 215 40. The airplane was boarded and we were at departure time and it even seemed that the mechanics were under pressure to sign the aircraft off and get it pushed off the gate.
ASRSN:2162294.s: The flight crew departed ZZZZ with a suspected brake fan issue on wheel #3, which maintenance signed off despite uneven temperatures. During landing at XXL, the aircraft veered left due to ineffective right-side brakes, requiring manual control to prevent a runway excursion.

ASRSN:2162348.n: Forgot to set brake for disconnect after push. After push and during starting engine number two, we received a 'R Start Abort' Caution message. I asked the ground crew to not disconnect as we may have an issue, and to standby. I pulled out the QRH and ran the procedure. After running the procedure, the number two engine started normally. At that point I instructed the push crew that they could disconnect. My attention at that point was focused on the FO starting engine number one as we had just received a fault on engine number 2. During that time I looked up to notice that the airplane was rolling forward and hit the tow-bar. I immediately pressed the brakes and set the parking brake. I motioned to the push crew to see if everyone was okay. They gave a signal that I presumed that everyone and everything was okay. The push crew then continued to pull back from the aircraft and gave the salute to taxi. Cause: The cause of the event was diverting from company SOP due to receiving a Caution message during the startup of engine number two. Normal procedure it to stay heads up, outside the aircraft. Once push has been completed, 'Set brakes, clear to disconnect.' When we got the Caution message my attention was diverted. And when I asked the push crew not to disconnect, I neglected to set the brakes as part of SOP. After we ran the QRH and I instructed the push crew to disconnect, my thought process was that I had already set the brakes as part of SOP. The added caution message event derailed me from my normal flow. Furthermore, my attention was diverted inside the aircraft during engine start number 1 because of the caution message received during engine start number one. Because of those two factors, I didn't immediately notice that the airplane had started to roll forward. Suggestions: Whenever an event grabs my attention and disrupts SOP, stop, go slow and return to the beginning of SOP to make sure everything was accomplished properly. Aircraft rolled forward after tow-bar disconnect due to parking brake not being set.Ground crew headset was not working, so the flight crew and push coordinator briefed face to face about using the OPs frequency for verbal communication during the pushback. During the push we were cleared to start engines verbally. Captain asked for the engine starts, right then left. During the right engine start, we received a R Start Abort" caution just as the tug came to a stop at the end of the push. The Captain advised the ground crew we had an engine issue and to remain connected. I confirmed the caution message and the Captain ran the QRH for a R Start Abort. After completing the QRH, the Captain asked for a second start attempt. I initiated the right engine start, and the engine completed its start cycle normally this time. I followed this with a left engine start. I believe hearing, during the left engine start, the Captain say to the tug-driver that we had one good engine start and they were good/clear to disconnect. I do not recall the exact phraseology he used. While watching the left engine start indication I noticed the driver waving his hands and give an over hand "X" or stop command. Noticing the airplane slowing rolling forward I yelled brakes and simultaneously applied the toe brakes. I'm not sure if my application or the Captain's brought the airplane to a stop but it seems we had rolled about 1-3 feet forward. At this time 2 ground personnel, one from each side of the nose wheel appeared moving in a forward and outward direction from the nose wheel in what appeared to be shock/surprise that the airplane was moving. I'm not certain to the position of the tow bar in relation the the tug or the aircraft as it is not is line of sight at this point. After the airplane came to a stop and the tug driver confirmed the brakes were set, the ground crew finished their duties under the nose and gave the all clear. The Captain asked and confirmed that no one was hurt or injured. As there were no indications that the airplane hit or ran into anything and only moved due to the parking brake not being set, we finished the checklists, and continued the flight.Cause: Failure to set the parking brake after the push due to the distraction or a "R Start Abort" caution message occurring during the pushback.Suggestions: I could have been more proactive/assertive in completing the required QRH for the start abort rather than allowing the Captain to do it. As we were at a complete stop and still attached to the towbar, I felt it wasn't a big deal that the Captain reached for the QRH and began the checklist. I feel this was a contributing factor as to why he forgot to set the parking brake.Even though I was in the middle of the Left engine start when he told the tug driver to disconnect, I cannot recall hearing "Parking Brake set, cleared to disconnect". Even as it isn't required for the FO to verify the brakes are engaged, we should have the natural tendency to double check, or verify, each others work and tasks. While we (the flight deck and the tug driver) did have 2 way communication through the use of his handheld radio and the ops frequency. I believe it was different enough from standard operations that the tug driver used hand signals to get our attention to the aircraft movement rather than the radio he was holding. I think if he had a standard headset it would have been second nature to just say what he saw."
ASRSN:2162348.s: Flight crew forgot to set the parking brake after pushback due to distraction from a right engine start abort caution. The aircraft rolled forward and struck the tow-bar before stopping, with no injuries reported.

ASRSN:2162351.n: We were flying from ZZZ1 to ZZZ at FL190. As we were about to descend on the ZZZZZ arrival, we received a red CAS message, R ENG OIL PRESS LOW;" followed by the aural alarm. As I was retrieving the QRH, we were cleared to descend via the arrival. We began our descent, and I read out the checklist, which called for the right engine to be shut down. We told ATC about our situation and continued with the associated checklists. As we were reaching the final altitude on the arrival, ATC gave [priority handling] to us. We coordinated with the tower and emergency personnel about the situation, asking them to check the right engine upon landing. An emergency vehicle would follow us on the runway. We landed on runway XXL and taxied back to the FBO, where we entered and were met with the fire engine and emergency personnel. Upon a visual examination of the engine, we could see a large quantity of oil along the nacelle and the back fuselage of the airplane. The oil continued leaking on the ramp. Cause: I believe the improper installation of the oil cap on the right engine was the reason for this. The oil cap was locked down, but there was a chain connected to the oil cap to keep it from falling when oil was being replaced that was installed inside the oil reservoir neck and attached from the inside of the oil reservoir neck to the outside cap. This did not seem to allow a tight seal for the oil cap when in the down and locked position. However, I am not privy to how the cap was before the maintenance or in the mind of the maintenance official, so I'm unsure exactly the cause of the oil leak.Suggestion: If the oil cap chain was improperly installed, ensuring that maintenance personnel do not install it that way would be the primary step in preventing this event from occurring again. A secondary step would be to have pilots ensure that the chain is not in the way of the seal during oil inspection."
ASRSN:2162351.s: The flight crew experienced a right engine oil pressure low warning at FL190 while descending on the ZZZZZ arrival, forcing an engine shutdown and emergency landing on runway XXL. The pilot attributed the leak to an improperly installed oil cap chain preventing a tight seal, though the exact maintenance cause remained uncertain.

ASRSN:2162358.n: Upon reaching cruise altitude FL 330, the left engine Fan Vib (Vibration) indicator read 2.9, the vibration could be felt on the yoke and we could hear it. FO remained PF, I ran the QRC/QRH. Because of the excessive vibration, possibility of damage and the need to reduce airspeed and altitude I decided to [request priority handling] with ATC prior to completing the QRH procedure. Before reducing thrust to idle I opted to descend to FL 250 and slow. At FL 250 and 250 KIAS vibrations were 2.0, we reduced left engine to idle IAW (In Accordance With) QRH then increased to normal thrust with no correction to vibration. We reduce the left thrust enough to reduce Vib to 1.7. We were able to maintain altitude and airspeed at this setting without increasing the right engine thrust. I decided to keep the [priority] status with ATC and continue to ZZZ. In the descent vibration decreased. We landed [Runway] XXC, deployed thrust reversers and Vib increased to 1.8, exited the runway, cancelled the [priority handling] and taxied to the gate with no further issues. Notifications were made IAW FOM X.X.XCause: An excessive van vib indication led me to suspect engine damage. I [request priority handling] with ATC, completed to QRH, and continued to land in ZZZ.Suggestion: Review and consider a change to the QRH verbiage. Specifically the caution note between steps XX and YY. I believe that note will potentially cause pilots to skip step XY, in the way it is written. My recommended change would be along the lines of, A reduction to idle thrust at high altitudes may cause a loss of airspeed or altitude. Before initiating step XY ensure aircraft is at a safe altitude"."
ASRSN:2162358.s: The crew experienced excessive left engine fan vibration at FL 330, prompting a priority descent to FL 250 and thrust reduction per QRH. They landed safely at ZZZ with vibration decreasing during descent, though it briefly increased during reverse thrust deployment.

ASRSN:2162417.n: During pushback from gate XX, received Breakaway call from push crew. Aircraft was accelerating in reverse as gate has downhill tilt. Brakes applied and aircraft came to an abrupt stop.. several Flight Attendants (f/a) reported getting tossed and contacting rear galley with moderate force. I suggested they go to medical. They refused and continued on to ZZZ1. Had maintenance perform nose gear inspection. We were pushing back, when apparently our plane felt like we had hit something very hard or something hit us hard like we had crashed or ran into something. It was awfully scary! Our plane jerked back and forth and side to side in an erratic motion. Also it felt like the plane tilted and lost its balance! Flight attendants were thrown in the back and held each other until the plane came to a stop. We were told that the tug had broken while pushing or pulling the plane back. I was in the back galley with other flight attendants making sure we are ready, cabin secured, galley secured for our take off because my position is the the Aft Galley.I fell backwards towards the ovens, as the plane violently shook forward and back, side to side while I was trying to hang on and catch another flight attendant. It felt like I was in a bad car accident, my neck and lower back started to feel some aches and stiffness as we continued on our flight.Peramedics met the plane along with our Supervisor.
ASRSN:2162417.s: During pushback, a downhill gate caused the aircraft to accelerate in reverse after the tug reportedly broke, resulting in an abrupt stop. Several flight attendants were thrown with moderate force, sustaining neck and back pain, though they refused medical attention and continued the flight.

ASRSN:2162479.n: During preflight we received a NOTOC for dry ice. During pushback our load closeout did not show any restricted articles. We radioed Operations and Operations said that the dry ice was NOT loaded, to use load closeout, and to disregard the NOTOC. We completed flows and checklists and were cleared for takeoff. At about that time we started receiving ACARS messages but ignored them while in sterile. Upon reaching 10k ft., we read and acknowledged the messages which told us that the NOTOC was actually valid and that our load closeout had been deleted. Several minutes later we received [another] load closeout that included the restricted article. Cause: Central Load Planning was obviously confused what was loaded in our airplane. Mitigation suggestion: if Load Planning wants to delete a NOTOC, an official ACARS should be required. Either way, we need to have an official reconciliation of the discrepancy between the received NOTOC and load closeout.
ASRSN:2162479.s: The flight crew received conflicting dry ice documentation during pushback and takeoff, relying on Operations' verbal instruction to disregard the NOTOC. Central Load Planning's confusion caused a valid restricted article to be omitted from the initial load closeout, requiring an official reconciliation of the discrepancy.

ASRSN:2162488.n: GPS Jamming and Spoofing Event: GPS updating of the FMC position was inhibited during departure. After takeoff the EICAS advisory messages 'Transponder L' and 'Transponder R' started to display periodically. On the Control Display Unit (CDU) it was seen that the GPS position was rejected and displayed as blank intermittently. At times it was noted that when GPS position was displayed, this position corresponded to the location of OJAM Airport, despite that the aircraft was located over the Mediterranean Sea. Once clear of the affected area, GPS updating was activated and the flight completed normally.
ASRSN:2162488.s: During departure over the Mediterranean Sea, GPS jamming and spoofing inhibited FMC position updates and caused intermittent transponder advisories. The GPS displayed a false position at OJAM Airport until the aircraft cleared the affected area, allowing normal flight completion.

ASRSN:2162489.n: GPS Jamming and/or Spoofing Event: In cruise, on the airway L550 approaching the Sinai Peninsula area, GPS updating of the FMC position was inhibited from prior position OBNAK. Approaching position KITOT, the EICAS advisory messages 'Transponder L' and 'Transponder R' started to display periodically. On the Control Display Unit (CDU) it was seen that the GPS position was rejected and displayed as blank intermittently - radio updating was functioning correctly and ANP was maintained at approximately 0.40. The route continued on Airway N697 and then L667 across Egypt, then M872 to METRU exit point from the FIR (Flight Information Region). Once out of the Egyptian airspace, GPS updating was activated and the flight completed normally.
ASRSN:2162489.s: During cruise over the Sinai Peninsula, a flight crew experienced GPS jamming or spoofing that inhibited FMC position updates and triggered intermittent transponder advisories. GPS updating resumed normally after exiting Egyptian airspace, allowing the flight to complete without further incident.

ASRSN:2162528.n: Separate preflight inspections performed by both Student Pilot (SP) and Flight Instructor (IP). No abnormal conditions noted, nor water/debris observed in fuel samples. Oil levels checked, IP noticed engine oil near max line but within acceptable limit. Engine cowling and exhaust openings looked clean, no leaks or abnormal residue observed by either crew member.During climb out, SP and IP both verbalized the recognition of an abnormal vibration and roughness from the engine, which could also be felt strongly in both sets of rudder pedals. IP took controls and notified ATC of possible engine roughness.ATC instructed to enter right downwind for runway XXR(shortened), cleared to land. Vibration continued during flight in the pattern, IP landed aircraft safely on XXR and taxied back to the ramp, no additional abnormal conditions or annunciations observed by crew while in flight or during taxi. No further assistance provided or necessary from ATC.After engine shutdown, IP performed an additional inspection of the engine compartment, and observed visible wet oil in the exhaust opening on lower surface of the engine cowling and on the nose wheel strut.
ASRSN:2162528.s: A Student Pilot and Flight Instructor experienced engine vibration and roughness during climb-out in a single-engine aircraft. Post-landing inspection revealed wet oil on the exhaust and nose strut, indicating an oil leak not detected during preflight checks.

ASRSN:2162678.n: Shortly after reaching top of climb received Level 1 TNK 1 Tip Fuel Lo alert, followed within a minute by TNK 3 Tip Fuel Lo alert. Ran QRH, no help. While troubleshooting these oddly concurrent alerts (and discussing that our jet had recently completed several days of maintenance) and coordinating with Dispatch and Maintenance Control via ACARS, we discovered that we were now showing approx 6000 lbs low to flight plan, less than 20 minutes after we'd noted 2000 lbs positive at TOC. Maintenance Control sent an ACARS that stated that their computers were telling them our jet was currently faulting tanks 1 and 3 fuel floats. As a crew we began to discuss the issue (summary of the situation, recommendations based on what we knew at that time, and comfort levels) - and whether it was it possibly only an indication error, or if our fuel numbers might possibly be grossly in error, even prior to refueling? Also, if necessary, what our divert alternatives and preferences might be? After a period of a few minutes we seemed to recover" a few thousand lbs of fuel, though we were still inexplicably low on gas relative to our flight plan and earlier readings (between 3 and 4 thousand pounds low to plan as I recall). We called Dispatch via SATCOM to discuss these issues and divert options if that became necessary. Moments later we received a Level 2 Fuel QTY/USED CHK alert - a primary alert for possible fuel leak, and initially ran that checklist up to the point of isolating the fuel tanks to determine the probable source of any leaks (none immediately apparent - fuel state didn't worsen relative to plan, although it was still a few thousand pounds low), after which we again SATCOMed Dispatch, asking for Maintenance Control to join, and requesting our Chief Pilot as well. As a flight crew we suspected that it was a gauging error, but also had no way of knowing with confidence whether our ramp load of fuel was also grossly inaccurate (based on previous block-in fuel - our gauge were clearly suspect). While discussing with Dispatch and Maintenance Control, one of the Maintenance Control representatives on the call informed us that their system was presently indicating our jet had between 6 and 7000 lbs of fuel remaining in each main tank (at this point was also showed approx 10,000 indicating in the aux after being transferred forward from the tail tank). If Maintenance Control's information was correct we'd possibly/probably have flamed out prior to reaching ZZZ. Coupled with the previous strange fuel indications and alerts, and considering that the jet had recently completed several days of intensive maintenance, our decision to divert was clear at this point. Because Dispatch was on the call when we learned of Maintenance Control's fuel indications, we were able to rapidly coordinate with our dispatcher the optimal and nearest divert at that point (ZZZ1). We disconnected the call with a plan, contacted ATC, summarized our situation, obtained new clearance direct ZZZ1, and [requested priority handling]. Landed ZZZ1 safely, indications on final suggested weight approximately correct, although initial drip stick readings by maintenance suggest gauging error in #2 tank by between 2300 and 4000 lbs low. Float faults in tank 1 and 3 still unexplained."
ASRSN:2162678.s: The flight crew experienced multiple fuel low alerts and a fuel leak warning shortly after top of climb, suspecting a gauging error following recent maintenance. They diverted to ZZZ1 after Maintenance Control indicated critically low fuel levels, landing safely with post-flight checks confirming a significant gauge error in tank 2.

ASRSN:2162686.n: Our flight was planned to depart runway 35 in MTJ back to ZZZ1. After getting our takeoff clearance from Denver center we were cleared to depart. Made a CTAF call and pulled out on runway for departure. Upon lining up with the runway the FO stated is that an airplane down there" I agreed with him and continued the roll to take the next runway exit. The aircraft that pulled out onto 17 after we pulled out on 35 did not make any CTAF announcements. We tried queuing them after pulling off with no answer. Another aircraft on CTAF who was doing pattern work stated they could see the twin engine down by 17. After the twin took off we taxied back around for a 35 departure again. The other aircraft never made a call.Busy non towered airport with an aircraft not communicating on CTAF. Build a tower and aircraft should be communicating on the field."
ASRSN:2162686.s: The crew at non-towered MTJ observed a twin-engine aircraft enter Runway 17 without CTAF communication while they were lining up on Runway 35. The reporter attributed the incident to the other pilot's failure to communicate and recommended building a tower.

ASRSN:2162700.n: F/O was pilot flying. ZZZ was advertising ILS XX, wind 310/10 gust 18. The approach became unstable around at 700 feet with speed of plus 20 and rate of descent more than 1000 feet. Executed go around, terrain terrain pull up pull up warning came after few seconds of go around. Tower gave vectors for climb to 4000 and finally 6000 from approach. I carried out the approach on 2nd time, realized that Low Time F/O's are not authorized to conduct approach landing and take off in special qualification airport. I did the ILS XX and landed. Pireps reported to ATC.Be familiar with Special Qualification Airport specially when flying with Low time F/O. Today we had to perform a go-around. We were performing the ILS XX into ZZZ. I was pilot flying, captain monitored. Winds were choppy and gusting. We chose [runway] XX as winds were near straight down the runway, and ATC advertised [runway] XX. Winds were around 310 10 gust 16. Autopilot was engaged, LOC and glide slope were captured. We started to experience speeds of plus/minus 15 knots, due to gusts over the mountains. Winds became far too strong, and changed in velocity rapidly. I had to constantly change power setting to stay on speed, as the attitude was oscillating greatly. Decent rate became far too high. We eventually experienced a pull up pull up annunciation as the autopilot could not keep up with the changes. We were fully configured flaps 45 by 1000 feet. Captain called a go around, and we went around. We came to realize after that ZZZ being a special qualification I as a low time FO cannot make takeoffs or landings. This went over our heads initially because I had told him I had just went into ZZZ and landed a few weeks back. It was my mistake that I had forgotten that was okay only in OE (Operating Experience). I forgot this isn't OE (Operating Experience) anymore, and I should not have been pilot flying. Captain assumed control once we were at a suitable altitude. And gave us 4000 ft initially then 6,000 ft, vectors back to [runway] XX. he came around and landed. He did not use autopilot on the second attempt and also experienced speed changes due to the winds, but was able to make a stable approach to land. I did not make any landing or the following takeoff into ZZZ, but we realized after the go around low time FO cannot do special qualification.Gust wind over mountains on approach end of runway XX into ZZZ. Confusion between us by me stating I had gone into ZZZ and landed during OE (Operating Experience) recently. I should have remembered the Captain is not OE (Operating Experience) qualified and that I cannot make the landing.We followed go around procedure and approach stability criteria. I believe we made the safe and right decision in going around. As far as us missing the low time FO restriction initially, I think I confused the Captain by telling him I was a low time FO but I had gone into ZZZ recently. Be more familiar with low time FO restrictions and special qualification airports.
ASRSN:2162700.s: A low-time First Officer flying an ILS approach into ZZZ executed a go-around due to unstable speed and descent caused by gusty winds over mountains. The crew later realized the First Officer was not authorized to land at this special qualification airport, so the Captain took control and completed the landing.

ASRSN:2162706.n: Dual MFD (Multi-Function Display) failureWhile climbing on departure from ZZZ1, DISPLAY COOL caution message showed on EICAS. FO was Pilot Flying and CA was Pilot Monitoring. I announced Display cool caution msg and FO called for QRC, QRH for DISPLAY COOL msg. I referenced and went through DISPLAY COOL QRH and do the procedure, msg went away and did not occurred in the next 45 minutes. While on cruise MFD 1 failed and as FO was already PF, I decided to keep it that way and run MFD FAILURE checklist and was not able to reset the MFD, in that moment ATC indicated to fly direct ZZZZZ fix a few moments later ATC asked if we were flying to the fix as we were flying on a heading around some weather. I advised we were troubleshooting our display screens and we might need advise from them to see if we were flying to the fix, they responded yes moments later. After we were flying to ZZZZZ MFD2 failed and once again run MFD fail checklist without a successful reset. Then few minutes later DISPLAY COOL showed again and run respective checklist again this time msg did not extinguished after 60 Seconds. Checklist mentioned land at nearest suitable airport and a note mentioning All displays will keep functioning for at least 30 minutes after fan failure I decided to take control of aircraft and [request priority handling] as we will need assist with navigation as we could lost all screens in the airplane. I asked FO to advise Flight Attendants and not to do a PA as I discussed with FO about two MFD failure as at that moment was not necessary for a PA, in case we would lost full screens we would make an announcement, we sent ACARS messages to Maintenance and Dispatch about situation and advised we might need to divert and as we were on the descent to ZZZ we decided to continue and Dispatch also agreed with continuing to destination. ATC was helpful providing vectors to ZZZ and flew a normal to RWY XXR ILS to a normal and stable landing taxied to gate with no more incidents and called Maintenance, Dispatch and Chief Pilot upon reaching gate.
ASRSN:2162706.s: During cruise, the Captain and First Officer experienced sequential dual MFD failures and a persistent DISPLAY COOL caution on a ZZZ1 departure. The crew executed checklists, requested priority handling, and diverted to ZZZ for a normal ILS landing after ATC provided navigation assistance.

ASRSN:2163018.n: Aircraft X, Pilot reported T2 sensor inop, went to aircraft with two other techs 1 and 2. Deferred the sensor, tech 1 started paperwork for the discrepancy. After that pilot told us minor bird strike, and pilot also stressed about leaving ZZZ. PILOT pressured tech 1 into return to service (RTS) BEFORE airport operations arrived. Tech 1 called Maintenance Control and had RTS, while me and tech 2 inspected the LH WING. After airport operations took sample, me and tech 2 and airport operations visually inspected the engine and noticed the damaged fan blade. And verbally confirmed this plane cannot go into service, at this time jet bridge was pulled and aircraft doors were closed. Tech 1 don't wait for us and then had out of service (OTS) the aircraft.Suggestions: Comply with airport operations and communicate with team members before RTS the aircraft. Day 0 approximately XA:45 me and my 2 other colleagues arrived to the gate pilot reported e1 t2 sensor fail due to the fact we didn't have enough time to fix the problem we decided to put the t2 sensor on MEL. While working on the deferral the pilot performed his walk around before boarding notice a bird strike on the left side leading edge of the slats. Me and one of my colleagues came down to perform a bird strike inspection and called airport operations to come and take there samples and perform there own job. In the mean time my other colleague stayed in the aircraft completing the deferral also pilot had not written up the bird strike in the log book and had asked him to do so. At this point both of us visually inspected the surrounding areas above and under the wing as well as the leading edge for any damage no damage was noted. The bird strike residue was from back of the slat track underneath the wing and out bored also to the side of the pylon. From a visual inspection it only seemed that there was only one bird strike. We both performed visual inspection of engine 1 and surrounding area no residue or damage was noted. Before cleaning the residue airport operations had arrived to take its samples my colleague came down to confirm that there was no damage and no damage was noted. I believe he had signed off the aircraft for service and called Maintenance Control of the bird strike that no damage was noted. Ground crew and flight crew was just waiting for us to clean the residue so the aircraft can push back from the gate. Approximately 2 minutes after the aircraft was put back to service we performed additional inspection on the engine to make sure the residue on the pylon was from the same bird strike that struck the leading edge of the slats. As inspecting each blade we notice on fan blade was bent which made the aircraft unsafe. He immediately called Maintenance Control that there was another bird strike the went in the engine 1 ending up on the pylon and seemed to be only one bird strike from the slats. The second birth strike made it past the engine through the bypass on to the pylon. Before the aircraft was pushed back we was able to contact the pilot thought the ground crew head sets that the aircraft is out of service due to the damage blade. At this point we opened the cowling to perform additional inspection of the engine according to bird strike inspection. Suggestions: What I learned from this occurrence is that always take your time to perform any inspection on aircraft and not allow any people to come in your way of rushing your job. Make sure you sign for the work you performed and don't trust anyone to sign for it if you didn't performed the work. I'm willing to learn from this and to keep our aircraft safe and airworthy.
ASRSN:2163018.s: Mechanics reported that a pilot pressured a colleague to return Aircraft X to service after a bird strike before airport operations arrived. A subsequent inspection revealed a damaged fan blade, forcing the aircraft out of service and highlighting the risks of rushing inspections under crew pressure.

ASRSN:2163041.n: This morning doing my monthly reports I found paperwork that was not shipped out for HAZMAT. I sent the info to the HAZMAT department on the undeclared paperwork that was shipped out yesterday for two fire extinguishers.Suggestions: I have talked and explained the importance of all HAZMAT materials that we carry here in ZZZ. I explained to other submitter the importance to question HAZMAT shipments going out if they are not sure. I received a call from AOG that two fire extinguishers and two batteries needed to go out to ZZZ1, and that they would send me the information for the courier about what time they would come and pick up the materials. I never received that information and the courier ended up coming before the items were prepared. So I sent them out via the courier and wasn't aware that the fire extinguishers needed to be sent out HAZMAT regardless of the courier until after it was already sent.Suggestions: My Supervisor had a talk with me this morning about the importance of all hazard material in ZZZ. My Supervisor explained to me in the future if I'm not sure on HAZMAT shipping , I should question it and contact my Supervisor and or materials training.
ASRSN:2163041.s: A ground employee shipped two fire extinguishers via courier to ZZZ1 without proper HAZMAT documentation because they were unaware of the requirement and did not receive pickup details from AOG. The supervisor subsequently instructed the employee to question uncertain HAZMAT shipments and contact training or management for clarification.

ASRSN:2163064.n: A tube of HAZMAT sealant was taken on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 rather than being shipped. Sealant was signed out from Parts and neither the mechanics or parts keepers caught the HAZMAT indication.Suggestions: Highlight the importance of HAZMAT items and parts and make better labels for HAZMAT items or something to make them pop."" I went on a road trip to ZZZ1 to fix a strobe light not flashing. Due to panels that needed to be removed, it was necessary to use sealant. When I was picking up parts for the road trip I was given sealant to take with me. I mentioned we were taking a repo flight and asked if it was fine we take it, the Parts employees said yes. About an hour later I boarded the repo flight and we left for ZZZ1. The trip to ZZZ1 was routine and we used the sealant as normal. When we returned, a Parts employee mentioned we should not have flown with it and it was supposed to be shipped. I asked if it was an issue and if I needed to do anything, they said it was fine.
ASRSN:2163064.s: A mechanic flew a tube of HAZMAT sealant on a repo flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 after Parts staff incorrectly approved it for transport instead of shipping. The sealant was used to repair a strobe light, and although Parts later noted the error, they stated no further action was required.

ASRSN:2163076.n: Person A prepared lithium metal batteries for shipment utilizing the HAZMAT shipping option. Person A used a UN specification box to ship the hazardous materials but covered up the UN markings on the box stating due to no packing group associated with UN 3090, a UN specification box was not needed. The package was rejected by the Company and returned. HAZMAT department was immediately notified and all documentation and pictures were sent. HAZMAT department reviewed the documentation and photos and gave clearance to reship with supervision signature. The HAZMAT was repackaged and shipped but not signed by leadership due to end of day operations for leadership. The package was rejected once again by the Company and returned at which time all documentation and pictures were sent to department immediately. Company cited that UN 3090 shipments must be inside a UN specification box.Suggestions: Possible re-training and reminder to pay attention to all the details provided within the IATA, Dangerous Goods (DG) department, and on the Shipper's Declaration.
ASRSN:2163076.s: Person A shipped lithium metal batteries (UN 3090) in a UN box with covered markings, causing two rejections by the Company for non-compliance. The HAZMAT department cleared reshipment with supervision, but the package was rejected again due to a missing leadership signature.

ASRSN:2163156.n: ZZZ shipped loaned tool, HAZMAT UN 3363, 1956, 3481, undeclared and without a Dangerous Goods (DG) form to ZZZ1 via the daily courier on Day 0. At approximately XA:00 Day 0, Maintenance was let into the parts room with the tool at which time the Technician rolled the tool case to the courier staging area and stated it needed to go back to ZZZ1 that night. Staff on shift did not follow up to ensure there was a DG form created to move the tool and just loaded the tool with the rest of the items when the daily courier arrived, therefore leading to the undeclared shipment of HAZMAT.Suggestions: Retrain of all staff in materials that nothing moves without a DG form, especially when a part or tool is handed off by Maintenance with no paperwork, those situations should always be questioned. Retrain on the process of creating a DG form when needed and proper contacts and procedures if unsure on proper steps. Additional instructions and training for staff on how to handle movement of loaned tools.
ASRSN:2163156.s: Maintenance staff and shift personnel shipped an undeclared HAZMAT loaned tool via daily courier without a Dangerous Goods form. The incident occurred because staff failed to verify paperwork when the tool was handed off, resulting in an improper shipment.
